The Andean parakeet, Bolborhynchus orbygnesius, is a small neotropical parrot whose life-history strategy reflects the constraints of its montane environment. Data from captive colonies indicate that eggs incubated at a constant temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C] will hatch after approximately 21.5 days [ab = approximately 21.5 days], a developmental period largely consistent with that documented in the congeneric species Bolborhynchus lineola. This modest starting mass necessitates an intensive period of biparental provisioning and rapid somatic growth within the nest cavity.

Adult females of the Andean parakeet attain a definitive body size that is modest for the genus, with the ultimate wet weight for females recorded at 43 grams [Wwi = 43 grams]. This asymptotic mass represents a substantial increase from the neonatal state and is consistent with the relatively slow growth trajectory observed in many montane bird species, where metabolic constraints imposed by cooler ambient temperatures and seasonally variable food availability may limit daily energy intake. The nestlings reach the fledging stage, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and departure from the nest cavity, at approximately 32 days since birth [tx = approximately 32 days since birth] at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. Following fledging, the young birds enter a prolonged period of post-fledging dependence and somatic growth. Such a strategy, combining a protracted developmental period with a low annual fecundity, is a common pattern among psittacines inhabiting seasonal montane habitats where food resources fluctuate markedly between breeding seasons and where the costs of nest site competition are high.
